commonMistakes: Saying closures copy variables instead of capturing them by reference.
Confusing closures with scope in general, or with the module pattern specifically.
detailedAnswer: A closure is a function combined with the lexical environment where it was created. When the outer function returns, variables it declared would normally be discarded, but if an inner function still references them, the environment stays alive. This is how callbacks retain state, how factory functions create private state, and how event handlers remember the data they were created with. Each call to the outer function creates a fresh environment, so closures created by different calls do not share state.
followUps: How would you use a closure to create private state?
What is the classic var-in-a-loop closure bug, and how does let fix it?
question: What is a closure in JavaScript? Give an example.
shortAnswer: A function that retains access to variables from the scope where it was created, even after the outer function has returned.
tips: Give a concrete example such as a counter factory, and explain that each call creates a fresh captured environment.
Mention a real use: callbacks, private state, or debouncing.
title: Closures

commonMistakes: Saying var is block-scoped, or that let is not hoisted at all (it is hoisted but in the temporal dead zone).
Claiming hoisting means the assignment moves, rather than the declaration.
detailedAnswer: var is function-scoped and hoisted with an initial value of undefined, so reading it before its line gives undefined rather than an error. let and const are block-scoped and also hoisted, but they live in the temporal dead zone between the start of the block and their declaration, so reading them early throws a ReferenceError. Function declarations are hoisted fully and can be called before their line; function expressions assigned to variables follow the rules of the variable kind. Modern code prefers const by default and let for reassignment, avoiding var entirely.
followUps: What is the temporal dead zone?
Why does a var loop variable break setTimeout callbacks, and how do you fix it?
question: Explain hoisting and the difference between var, let, and const.
shortAnswer: Declarations are processed before execution: var is function-scoped and initialised to undefined, while let and const are block-scoped and throw if used before declaration.
tips: Draw the temporal dead zone explicitly; interviewers check whether you know let is hoisted too.
Give the loop-with-setTimeout example as the practical consequence.
title: Hoisting, var, let, const

commonMistakes: Saying the event loop is what makes JavaScript multithreaded.
Forgetting that microtasks drain fully before the next macrotask.
detailedAnswer: JavaScript executes on a single thread: synchronous code runs to completion on the call stack. When the stack empties, the event loop takes work from task queues. Microtasks — promise reactions and queueMicrotask callbacks — drain completely before the next macrotask, which includes timers, I/O callbacks, and rendering steps. That is why a resolved promise callback runs before a setTimeout with delay zero, even if the timer was scheduled first. Long synchronous work blocks everything, including rendering and user input, because nothing else can run until the stack empties.
followUps: Why does a long loop freeze the page?
How do web workers fit into this picture?
question: How does the JavaScript event loop work, and why does a promise callback run before setTimeout(..., 0)?
shortAnswer: The call stack runs first, then all queued microtasks drain, and only then does the next macrotask (such as a timer) run.
tips: Walk through a short code example step by step rather than reciting definitions.
Name the queues explicitly: microtask queue versus macrotask queue.
title: The event loop

commonMistakes: Forgetting to check response.ok and treating every resolved fetch as success.
Not handling rejection, leaving unhandled rejections.
detailedAnswer: fetch returns a promise that rejects only on network failure, not on HTTP error statuses. A 404 or 500 response resolves normally, so code must check response.ok or response.status and throw or handle accordingly. For robust code, start independent requests together and await them with Promise.all, wrap awaits in try/catch, and pass an AbortSignal from an AbortController when the request should be cancellable — for example when a component unmounts or the user types a new query. Distinguish abort errors from real failures so cancellations do not show error messages.
followUps: How do you cancel a fetch?
When would you use Promise.allSettled instead of Promise.all?
question: How do you fetch data in JavaScript, and what are the common pitfalls?
shortAnswer: Use fetch with async/await, check response.ok because HTTP errors still resolve, handle rejections, and cancel with AbortController when the request becomes stale.
tips: Always mention response.ok — interviewers specifically look for it.
Bring up stale responses and cancellation for a stronger answer.
title: Fetching data with fetch

commonMistakes: Confusing event.target with event.currentTarget.
Calling stopPropagation when preventDefault was meant, or vice versa.
detailedAnswer: An event travels in three phases: capturing from the window down to the target, at the target, then bubbling back up. Listeners default to the bubbling phase. Event delegation exploits bubbling: a single listener on a parent inspects event.target to decide which child was involved, which is cheaper than a listener per child and works for elements added later. preventDefault stops the browser's default action, such as following a link or submitting a form; stopPropagation stops the event travelling further. They are independent and are often confused.
followUps: How would you implement delegation for a list with delete buttons?
What is the difference between debounce and throttle?
question: Explain event bubbling and event delegation. When would you use delegation?
shortAnswer: Events bubble from the target up through ancestors, so one parent listener can handle many children by checking event.target.
tips: Give a concrete example: a todo list with delete buttons, including dynamically added items.
State the target versus currentTarget distinction unprompted.
title: Event bubbling and delegation

commonMistakes: Saying TypeScript adds runtime type checking.
Using any to silence errors instead of fixing the underlying mismatch.
detailedAnswer: TypeScript adds a static type layer that is checked at compile time and then erased, so the shipped code is plain JavaScript with no runtime type checks. That is why runtime validation of external data is still necessary. any opts out of checking and lets errors through to runtime, while unknown is the safe alternative: it accepts any value but requires narrowing before use. Strict mode, especially strictNullChecks, is what makes the system genuinely useful, because without it null and undefined are assignable to everything.
followUps: When is any acceptable, and when should you use unknown instead?
How do you validate API data at runtime if types are erased?
question: What is the difference between any and unknown in TypeScript?
shortAnswer: any disables type checking; unknown accepts any value but forces you to narrow it before use.
tips: Mention type erasure: types never reach runtime, which is why unknown plus a runtime check is the safe pattern.
Say when you would actually use each one.
title: any versus unknown

commonMistakes: Saying interfaces and type aliases are interchangeable in all cases — aliases can name unions and tuples, interfaces can merge and extend.
Over-generifying a helper used in exactly one place.
detailedAnswer: A generic function or type declares type parameters, such as T, that callers supply implicitly through inference or explicitly. This preserves the relationship between inputs and outputs: a generic identity or first-element helper returns the caller's type, whereas an any-based version discards that information. Constraints with extends restrict what a type argument may be, so the implementation can safely use required properties. keyof combined with generics gives type-safe property access, and utility types such as Partial, Pick, and Omit replace duplicated hand-written variants.
followUps: How do you write a generic function that safely reads a property by key?
When is a generic the wrong tool, and what would you use instead?
question: What are generics in TypeScript, and why are they better than any for reusable helpers?
shortAnswer: Generics parameterise a function or type by type, so one implementation serves many types while preserving type information at each call site.
tips: Write a tiny example on the board, such as first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined.
Mention constraints and keyof to show depth beyond the basic definition.
title: TypeScript generics

commonMistakes: Typing children as JSX.Element, which rejects text and arrays.
Forgetting the element generic on event types, losing currentTarget properties.
detailedAnswer: Props are a plain object type, and children should be typed ReactNode, which covers elements, strings, numbers, fragments, arrays, and null — far wider than JSX.Element. Events use synthetic types parameterised by element, such as React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, which determines what currentTarget offers. useState infers its type from the initial value, so useState<User | null>(null) needs an explicit generic when the initial value is narrower than the real state. DOM refs start as null and must be checked. Generic components infer their type parameter from props at each use site, keeping reusable UI type-safe.
followUps: Why is React.FC discouraged in modern codebases?
How would you type a reducer's actions in a component?
question: How do you type React components, props, and events in TypeScript?
shortAnswer: Props as an object type, children as ReactNode, events as React synthetic types parameterised by element, and explicit generics where inference would be too narrow.
tips: Name ReactNode explicitly and explain why JSX.Element is too narrow.
Give the useState<User | null>(null) example.
title: Typing React with TypeScript

commonMistakes: Saying hooks can be conditional as long as the condition is stable — they cannot, because order must be identical on every render.
Omitting dependencies and debugging stale values instead of fixing the dependency array.
detailedAnswer: React tracks hooks by call order across renders, which is why they must be called unconditionally at the top level of a component or custom hook. A hook inside a condition or loop would shift the order of every later hook and attach state to the wrong hook. useState holds a value across renders and triggers re-renders when changed; useRef holds a mutable value without triggering renders; useEffect runs after commit and its cleanup runs before the next effect run and on unmount. Custom hooks reuse logic, not state — each component calling the hook gets its own independent state.
followUps: What is a stale closure, and how do missing effect dependencies cause one?
Why do effects run twice in React 18 Strict Mode development?
question: What are the rules of hooks, and why do they exist?
shortAnswer: Hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level, because React identifies them by call order across renders.
tips: Explain the mechanism (call order), not just the rule — that is what interviewers reward.
Mention the exhaustive-deps lint rule as the practical enforcement.
title: Rules of hooks

commonMistakes: Putting fetched data in plain useState and re-implementing caching badly.
Putting everything in one context and re-rendering the whole app on every change.
detailedAnswer: Start with local state and lift it only when another component needs it. useReducer centralises complex, interrelated updates as explicit actions, which is easier to test and reason about than scattered setters. Context passes values down without prop drilling but is not a state manager: it has no update mechanism and no selectors, so every consumer re-renders when the value changes. Fetched data is server state — a cache with loading, error, freshness, and invalidation concerns — and belongs in a server-state library rather than hand-rolled useEffect fetching. External stores with selectors suit frequently changing shared client state. Shareable state such as filters belongs in the URL.
followUps: How would you design state for a shopping cart versus a dashboard?
When would you choose Redux Toolkit over context?
question: How do you decide where state should live in a React application?
shortAnswer: Local by default; lift when shared, reduce when transitions are complex, context for rarely changing shared values, and a dedicated library for server state.
tips: Frame the answer by kind of state: local, shared, server, URL — not by library name.
Mention context's re-render behaviour explicitly.
title: State design in React

commonMistakes: Wrapping every component in memo without measuring.
Passing inline objects or functions to memoised children, silently defeating memoisation.
detailedAnswer: A component re-renders when its own state changes, its parent re-renders, or a consumed context changes; re-rendering is not the same as DOM updating, since React diffs first. React.memo skips re-rendering when props are shallowly unchanged, useMemo caches expensive computed values, and useCallback caches function identity so memoised children do not see a new prop every render. These only help when the work is expensive or when they prevent a large subtree from re-rendering, and they add comparison cost otherwise. The correct workflow is to profile first, fix the measured bottleneck — which may be bundle size, a network waterfall, or a huge list needing virtualization — and re-measure.
followUps: Why does an inline arrow function prop defeat React.memo?
How would you reduce a large initial bundle?
question: How do React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback work, and when should you not use them?
shortAnswer: They cache renders, values, and function identities respectively, but only pay off for expensive work or large subtrees — measure with the Profiler first.
tips: Explain the shallow, referential comparison — that is the key mechanic.
Name a non-render bottleneck (bundle size, lists) to show you optimise the right thing.
title: Memoization and React performance

commonMistakes: Using array indexes as keys for reorderable lists.
Assuming re-render means DOM update — React diffs first and usually changes little.
detailedAnswer: Rendering means calling a component to produce elements; committing means applying the diff to the DOM. React's reconciler matches the new tree against the previous one, using keys to identify list items across renders. Stable, unique keys let React reuse DOM nodes and preserved component state correctly when items are inserted, removed, or reordered; index keys tie identity to position, so reordering gives the wrong item the wrong state and focus. State itself is preserved by position in the tree, so moving a component to a different position resets its state even if its type is unchanged.
followUps: What happens to state when a component moves position in the tree?
How does React decide which DOM nodes to update?
question: How does React reconciliation work, and why do keys matter?
shortAnswer: React diffs the new element tree against the old one and patches only what changed; stable keys let it match list items correctly across renders.
tips: Use the reorderable list example to make the index-key failure concrete.
Distinguish rendering from committing.
title: Reconciliation and keys
